title: Taking apart and rebuilding
keyIdea: Many objects are made from a small set of pieces, like a tower of building blocks. You can take the object apart, and every piece is still there afterwards: nothing is used up, and the number of pieces stays the same. You can then put the same pieces together in a new way to make a new object, such as a bridge or a table. The new object has a new shape and can do a new job, but the pieces themselves have not changed: each block keeps its own size, colour and material. Because it is the same pieces, the new object weighs exactly the same as the old one, however tall, long or flat it is. A set of pieces can make many objects, but only ones that need the pieces you have: a kit with no wheels cannot make a car.
familyTip: Build a small tower or house from 6 to 10 bricks or blocks and count the pieces together. Take it apart, count again, then build something new from the same pieces. If you have kitchen scales, weigh it before and after. Ask: what changed, and what stayed the same?

visual.caption: A brick house is taken apart and built into a boat. Changed or the same? Drag each card into a box, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: take a tower apart and count, rebuild the pieces as a bridge, weigh all three, sort what changed, and check what a kit can build.

kid: Look at a tower made of 6 blocks. Take it apart, one block at a time. Count the blocks in the pile. There are still 6! Taking it apart does not use up any blocks.

Now use the same 6 blocks to build a bridge. You do not need any new blocks. You just put them together in a new way. The bridge has a new shape. It can do a new job too: a toy car can drive under it.
Weigh the tower. Then weigh the bridge. They weigh the same! It is the same blocks, so the weight cannot change. A long, flat shape is not heavier than a tall one.

The blocks do not change. The red block is still red and still made of wood. Only where each block goes is new. But you can only build what your blocks allow. With no wheels, you cannot make a car with wheels.
adult: Ages 7 to 8. NGSS 2-PS1-3 asks children to make observations and build an evidence-based account of how an object made of a small set of pieces can be taken apart and made into a new object. The idea behind it, PS1.A, is that a great variety of objects can be built from a small set of pieces. Key words: pieces, take apart, rebuild, object, shape, same.

This is an early step towards conservation of mass. Children see that the number of pieces and the total weight stay the same while the shape and use change. In England, it links to Year 2 Uses of everyday materials and to Year 1 and 2 working scientifically: observing closely and using simple equipment, such as scales.

Common mistakes: thinking some pieces are used up or lost when a model is taken apart; thinking a new object needs new pieces; expecting a longer, bigger or flatter model to weigh more; thinking the pieces themselves change, for example their colour or material; and thinking any set of pieces can build anything.

In the lab, children take a 6-piece tower apart and count the pieces. They rebuild the same pieces into a bridge from the bottom up. They weigh the tower, the loose pile and the bridge, sort what changed from what stayed the same, and decide which models a 4-block, 2-plank kit can build.

practice.prompt: Taking apart and rebuilding: Ben takes his 6-block tower apart. How many blocks are in the pile?
practice.hint: Did any block go away when he took the tower apart?
practice.explain: Taking a model apart does not use up any pieces, so all 6 blocks are still there.

practice.prompt: A brick house has {n} bricks. Mia takes it apart and builds a boat with all of the bricks. How many bricks are in the boat?
practice.hint: She used every brick from the house. Did the number change?
practice.explain: All {n} bricks went into the boat. The shape changed, but the number of bricks stayed the same.

practice.prompt: A tower of blocks weighs {g} g. It is rebuilt into a long, flat wall with the same blocks. How many grams does the wall weigh?
practice.hint: Same blocks, new shape. Does a new shape add any weight?
practice.explain: The wall is made of exactly the same blocks, so it weighs {g} g too. Shape does not change weight.

practice.prompt: A tower is rebuilt into a bridge. Which of these changed?
practice.hint: The blocks are the same. What is different about how it looks?
practice.explain: Only the shape (and the job it does) changed. The blocks, how many there are and their colours stayed the same.

practice.prompt: A kit has 4 blocks and 2 planks, but no wheels. Which can you build with it?
practice.hint: Check what pieces each one needs. Does the kit have them?
practice.explain: A table needs 4 blocks for legs and 2 planks for the top, which the kit has. A car needs wheels, and 10 blocks is too many.

pool.prompt: Sara wants to turn her brick castle into a rocket. What does she need?
choices: The same bricks, put together a new way
A whole new set of bricks
Glue to change the bricks' shape
pool.hint: Can the castle's bricks be used again?
pool.explain: She can take the castle apart and use the same bricks to build a rocket. No new bricks are needed.

pool.prompt: A tall tower and a long, low bridge are built from the same 6 blocks. Which weighs more?
pool.hint: Are there any extra blocks in either one?
pool.explain: They use the same 6 blocks, so they weigh the same. Changing the shape does not change the weight.

pool.prompt: A red block from a tower is used in a new bridge. What colour is it now?
choices: It changes to match the bridge
pool.hint: Does moving a block change the block itself?
pool.explain: It is still red. Rebuilding changes where each piece goes, not the pieces themselves.

pool.prompt: Why can a set of bricks make a house, a boat and a bridge?
choices: The same pieces can go together in many ways
The bricks change shape each time
pool.hint: Think about putting the same pieces in new places.
pool.explain: A small set of pieces can be arranged in many ways, so it can make many different objects.

pool.prompt: A model uses {a} blocks and {b} planks. It is taken apart. How many pieces are in the pile?
pool.hint: Every piece goes into the pile. Add the blocks and the planks.
pool.explain: {a} blocks and {b} planks make {=a+b} pieces. Taking it apart keeps every one of them.

pool.prompt: Each block weighs 10 g. A tower uses {n} blocks. How many grams does the tower weigh?
pool.hint: Add 10 g for every block, or multiply the number of blocks by 10.
pool.explain: {n} blocks of 10 g weigh {=10*n} g. A new model from the same blocks weighs {=10*n} g too.

pool.prompt: A new model needs 8 blocks, but your kit has only 5. What happens?
choices: You cannot build it with this kit
The 5 blocks will be enough if you squash them
pool.hint: Compare what the model needs with what you have.
pool.explain: You can only build what your pieces allow. 5 blocks are not enough for a model that needs 8.

pool.prompt: Jay takes a model apart and two pieces roll under the sofa. Are they gone?
choices: No, they are still pieces, just lost for now
Yes, taking apart used them up
Yes, pieces vanish when a model is taken apart
pool.hint: Taking apart does not make pieces disappear. Where are they?
pool.explain: The pieces still exist under the sofa. Find them and the pile has every piece again.

pool.prompt: A block tower is rebuilt into a bridge. What else changed besides its shape?
choices: What the blocks are made of
pool.hint: A tower stands tall. What can a bridge do?
pool.explain: The bridge can do a new job, like letting a toy car cross. The blocks and their material stayed the same.
